patient.chief_complaint: Binocular vertical diplopia and progressive limitation of eye elevation, initially treated as Brown syndrome
patient.hpi:
A 47-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and polycystic ovarian syndrome presented for re-evaluation of persistent and worsening binocular diplopia and restriction of eye elevation. Eight weeks prior to the current admission, she had noticed binocular vertical diplopia that was worst when looking to the right. Ophthalmology initially identified a left hypotropia of 4 prism diopters and mild limitation of elevation of the left eye in adduction, and made a diagnosis of acquired Brown syndrome (restriction of the superior oblique tendon sheath). She was started on ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily and later prednisolone 25 mg daily; she had some pain relief but persistent motility deficit.

Over the following month, the motility deficit progressed to bilateral moderate limitation of elevation in adduction. Two repeat MRI studies of the brain and orbits showed no superior oblique hypertrophy, tendon inflammation, or trochlear attachment abnormality. Serological testing for SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, and mixed connective tissue disease was negative. She continued on oral prednisolone up to 50 mg daily and later methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine without significant improvement.

Now, 8 months after the initial presentation, she has also developed bilateral upper eyelid ptosis (noticed by her husband over the past 3 weeks), increasing difficulty finishing a meal due to jaw fatigue, and a muffled nasal voice quality that worsens with prolonged speaking. She recalls that the ptosis seems more pronounced in the late afternoon. She has had no prior ophthalmic surgery or trauma. On examination, bilateral ptosis was now evident (right greater than left), along with bilateral restriction of elevation in adduction. The ice pack test applied for 5 minutes produced a 4 mm improvement in ptosis bilaterally. The SLURP test was positive for fatigable palate elevation.
pmh: Acquired Brown syndrome — diagnosed 8 months ago (under revision)

family_history: Mother had Hashimoto's thyroiditis; no family history of neuromuscular disease

social_history.note: Accountant; non-smoker; moderate alcohol use; married; no children; regular exercise prior to eye symptoms

physical_exam.general: Well-appearing; bilateral ptosis visible; cushingoid features mild (from prednisolone)
physical_exam.neurological: Bilateral ptosis (right > left). Positive ice pack test (4 mm improvement bilaterally). Bilateral restriction of elevation in adduction (left -2, right -1). No pain on eye movement. Cover test: left hypotropia 4 PD. No proptosis. Fatigable palate on SLURP test (positive). Jaw fatigue on prolonged chewing test. Cogan lid twitch sign positive. Neck flexor strength 4+/5 (fatigable). Limb strength 5/5. DTR 2+ symmetric. Sensation intact. No fasciculations.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.abdomen: Mild central adiposity (prednisolone effect); no organomegaly

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: AChR antibody–positive generalized myasthenia gravis, initially misdiagnosed as Brown syndrome (G70.01)

differential.key_features: Three consecutive normal orbital MRI studies; bilateral presentation (atypical for Brown syndrome); ptosis and bulbar symptoms developed — not explained by SO tendon pathology
differential.distinguishing_test: Orbital MRI (normal x3), ice pack test (positive), AChR antibody (positive)

differential.key_features: Normal TSH on levothyroxine; no proptosis; no lid retraction (ptosis is present — opposite sign); normal orbital muscles on MRI
differential.distinguishing_test: TSH (normal), orbital MRI (normal EOM), TRAb if needed

differential.key_features: ANA 1:160 is low-titer; anti-ds-DNA negative; no SLE criteria met; no complement consumption

optimal_actions.action: Reassess ice pack test in setting of progressive bilateral ocular motor signs not explained by structural pathology
MG antibody panel — AChR binding, blocking, modulating
Add pyridostigmine; transition from methotrexate to azathioprine; plan MGTX thymectomy

critical_actions: Recognize that bilateral adult-onset Brown syndrome not responding to treatment warrants MG workup
Positive ice pack test is key bedside test — >97% specific for MG ptosis
AChR antibody is diagnostic; negative orbital MRI x3 effectively excludes structural cause
Identify current medications (methotrexate, HCQ) were prescribed for incorrect diagnosis
Refer for thymectomy evaluation — patient meets MGTX criteria
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue immunosuppression for Brown syndrome when MG is diagnosed
Do not prescribe fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides
Do not miss the bulbar symptoms (jaw fatigue, nasal dysarthria) — these confirm generalized MG
key_reasoning_points: The diagnostic evolution: Brown syndrome is a reasonable diagnosis initially, but lack of MRI structural correlate and bilateral progression should prompt NMJ evaluation
Positive ice pack test and new ptosis are the pivotal clinical findings that change the diagnosis
Cogan lid twitch is highly specific for MG ptosis (98% specific)
AChR antibody 4.8 nmol/L with multi-muscle RNS decrement definitively confirms generalized MG
Polyautoimmune background (Hashimoto's, PCOS) increases risk of MG — should lower diagnostic threshold
Normal orbital MRI ×3 definitively excludes SO tendon pathology (Brown syndrome) and orbital myositis

red_herrings.finding: Prior Brown syndrome diagnosis with partial steroid response
red_herrings.why_misleading: Partial response to steroids and prior ophthalmology diagnosis creates anchoring bias toward connective tissue-related Brown syndrome
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Steroids also treat MG; partial steroid response is consistent with MG; bilateral onset in adults should trigger NMJ testing

red_herrings.finding: ANA 1:160 with polyautoimmune background suggesting SLE
red_herrings.why_misleading: Positive ANA + eye symptoms + joint involvement pattern could suggest SLE with ocular manifestations
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anti-ds-DNA negative, C3/C4 normal, SLE criteria not met; ANA is non-specific in polyautoimmune patients

red_herrings.finding: Hypothyroidism and PCOS suggesting thyroid-related ophthalmopathy
red_herrings.why_misleading: Thyroid disease is strongly associated with Graves' ophthalmopathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal TSH on levothyroxine; ptosis (not lid retraction); no proptosis; no EOM enlargement on MRI — Graves' ophthalmopathy excluded

metadata.condition_name: Generalized MG presenting as and initially misdiagnosed as acquired Brown syndrome
metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward (despite delayed diagnosis): positive ice pack test, Cogan twitch, AChR antibody, and multi-muscle RNS decrement all confirm MG; key is recognizing bilateral adult Brown syndrome as a MG mimic

mri.impression: Third consecutive normal orbital MRI; no trochlear or SO pathology; no intracranial lesion — structural causes definitively excluded. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS at orbicularis oculi, trapezius, deltoid

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi: Decrement 18% ABNORMAL
  Trapezius: Decrement 14% ABNORMAL
  Deltoid: Decrement 11% ABNORMAL

CONCLUSION: Multi-muscle decremental response confirms generalized MG.

output.impression: RNS: 18%, 14%, 11% decrement in three muscles — generalized NMJ dysfunction, confirms MG

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — EXTENSOR DIGITORUM COMMUNIS

MCD: 64 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
Blocking: 24% of potential pairs

CONCLUSION: SFEMG confirms NMJ dysfunction. Generalized MG.

output.report:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — PYRIDOSTIGMINE IN PATIENT ON METHOTREXATE + HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE

Query: Adding pyridostigmine to current regimen

FINDINGS:
  PYRIDOSTIGMINE + METHOTREXATE: No pharmacokinetic interaction; both can be maintained initially
  PYRIDOSTIGMINE + HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE: Case reports of HCQ mild benefit in MG; no adverse interaction
  HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE IN MG: Used off-label in refractory MG; some evidence for modest benefit; QTc monitoring required
  METHOTREXATE IN MG: Less commonly used for MG immunosuppression (azathioprine preferred); can be maintained if patient tolerating well

  ACTION PLAN: Add pyridostigmine 60 mg q6h; continue levothyroxine unchanged; transition from methotrexate to azathioprine for better MG evidence base; continue monitoring QTc on HCQ

CONCLUSION: Pyridostigmine safe to add. Recommend switching to azathioprine (TPMT testing required).
output.summary: Pyridostigmine safe with current regimen; transition methotrexate to azathioprine for better MG immunosuppression evidence

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Brown Syndrome vs Ocular MG — Diagnostic Pitfalls

KEY FINDINGS:
1. BROWN SYNDROME: Restriction of superior oblique tendon sheath causing limited elevation in adduction; typically unilateral; normal MRI shows no EOM enlargement; may be idiopathic, inflammatory, or traumatic
2. OCULAR MG: Can present identically to Brown syndrome with vertical strabismus and restricted elevation; key distinguishing features: ice pack test, fatigability, diurnal variation, Cogan lid twitch
3. BILATERAL BROWN SYNDROME: Rare; bilateral idiopathic form typically occurs in childhood; adult bilateral onset should trigger NMJ evaluation
4. CASE REPORTS: Multiple reports of MG initially diagnosed as Brown syndrome before NMJ testing; the progression to ptosis and bulbar symptoms is the clue
5. MANAGEMENT: Once MG confirmed, Brown syndrome medications (NSAIDs, immunosuppressants for connective tissue disease) are replaced by MG-specific treatment

CONCLUSION: MG should be excluded in all cases of acquired Brown syndrome, especially bilateral presentation in adults. Ice pack test and AChR antibody testing are essential.
output.summary: MG mimics Brown syndrome; bilateral adult-onset Brown syndrome should trigger NMJ evaluation; ice pack test and AChR antibody are key

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: MGTX Trial — Thymectomy in Non-Thymomatous Generalized MG

MGTX TRIAL (Wolfe GI et al., NEJM 2016):
  Population: AChR+ generalized MG patients aged 18-65 without thymoma
  Results: Thymectomy + prednisone vs prednisone alone
  Primary outcome: Thymectomy group had significantly lower quantitative MG score over 3 years
  Secondary outcome: Less prednisone required; fewer treatment failures; fewer hospitalizations
  THIS PATIENT: Age 47, AChR+ generalized MG, no thymoma → MGTX criteria met → thymectomy indicated

CONCLUSION: Patient meets MGTX trial criteria for thymectomy. Refer to thoracic surgery after MG optimization (IVIG or PLEX pre-operatively).
output.summary: MGTX trial supports thymectomy for AChR+ generalized MG aged 18-65; patient meets criteria; refer to thoracic surgery
